etymology: From Latin spiritualis, of the breath or spirit, from spiritus, breath. Webster 1828: consisting of spirit; not material; pertaining to the renewed nature of man; not carnal. In the Authorized Version spiritual never means vaguely religious. It means of the Holy Ghost — produced by Him, governed by Him, discerned by Him.
biblical_def: Spiritual in Scripture is not a temperament and not a level of religious interest. It is a description of what the Holy Ghost has done to a man. Paul draws the line without any middle ground: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man (1 Corinthians 2:14-15). Two categories, not three. The natural man is not less advanced; he is unable, and his inability is not intellectual but constitutional. The adjective attaches to whatever the Spirit produces and governs. The law itself is spiritual because the Spirit gave it: For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin (Romans 7:14). The resurrection body is a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not immaterial, but Spirit-animated and Spirit-sustained, which is why the same verse insists it is a body. Even the enemy is described this way: we wrestle against spiritual wickedness in high places (Ephesians 6:12). And the mark of the spiritual man is not ecstasy but meekness in restoring a fallen brother (Galatians 6:1). The word describes agency, not atmosphere.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPIRITUAL as consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal; mental, intellectual; and chiefly, pertaining to the renewed nature of man; not carnal or worldly; proceeding from the Holy Spirit; pure, holy, divine.
webster_full: SPIRITUAL, a. — Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal. Pertaining to the renewed nature of man; as spiritual life. Not carnal or worldly; not lustful. Proceeding from the Holy Spirit; as spiritual gifts. Pure; holy; divine.

Webster’s definition would not pass a modern editor, because it insists the word has a source. Proceeding from the Holy Spirit is the whole of it. In 1828 one could not be spiritual in general, any more than one could be royal in general; the adjective required a sovereign. That requirement is exactly what the last two centuries have removed.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 2:14
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
1 Corinthians 2:15
But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man.
Romans 7:14
For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal, sold under sin.
1 Corinthians 15:44
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
Galatians 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Ephesians 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
corruption_summary: Spiritual has been severed from the Holy Ghost and made a free-floating adjective for inwardness, so that a man may now call himself spiritual while denying the Spirit who alone makes anyone spiritual — the exact reversal of 1 Corinthians 2:14.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase spiritual but not religious is the finished product of a two-century project, and it is the precise inversion of Paul’s usage. In Scripture the word names a man acted upon by a Person; in current speech it names a man attending to himself. Webster still required a source — proceeding from the Holy Spirit. Detached from that source, spirituality becomes whatever the individual finds elevating, and the natural man of 1 Corinthians 2:14 is thereby able to describe himself with the very adjective Paul uses to exclude him. The corruption is not that unbelievers use the word loosely. It is that the church has adopted the loose sense, so that spiritual growth can be discussed at length without reference to the Holy Ghost, and spiritual disciplines can be taught as techniques for producing what only regeneration produces.

A second corruption runs inside the church and is older: the Corinthian error of treating spiritual as a rank. Paul is answering people who had already made it one, sorting the congregation by manifestation and eloquence. His correction is Galatians 6:1 — ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. The test of the spiritual man is what he does with a brother caught in sin, and the clause that follows puts him on notice about himself. Every movement that has graded believers into ordinary and Spirit-filled tiers, from the ancient enthusiasts to the modern apostle-and-prophet claims of the New Apostolic Reformation, has had to ignore that verse. The Spirit’s presence is proved by meekness and by submission to the closed canon, not by manifestation.

Third, a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) is persistently read as a non-physical body, which would make the resurrection a metaphor. Paul’s adjectives describe animating principle, not substance: the natural body is animated by the soul, the spiritual body by the Spirit. Both are bodies. The Lord ate broiled fish after He rose and invited Thomas to handle Him. The confession of the bodily resurrection of the just and the unjust stands or falls on refusing this misreading.
roots_summary: The New Testament’s spiritual is pneumatikos, an adjective built directly on pneuma, Spirit. Its opposites are two: psychikos, soulish or natural, and sarkikos, fleshly. Confusing those two opposites is the source of most bad teaching on this word.
roots_lines: Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; belonging to, produced by, or governed by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:15; 15:44; Ephesians 6:12).
Greek psychikos — soulish, natural; the man living by unrenewed human faculty (1 Corinthians 2:14, the natural man). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; the source of carnal in Romans 7:14, describing not the unregenerate man but the regenerate man’s remaining corruption.
The two contrasts are distinct: psychikos divides the unconverted from the converted; sarkikos divides the immature believer from the mature. Paul uses both in 1 Corinthians, two chapters apart.
usage: The natural man receiveth not and he that is spiritual judgeth all things (1 Corinthians 2:14-15) — two categories, no third.
The law is spiritual (Romans 7:14): the adjective attaches to what the Spirit authored, not to what the reader feels.
A spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) is Spirit-animated, not immaterial — still a body, or the resurrection is a figure of speech.

etymology: Old English gecynd, nature, race, offspring, from the same root as kin. Webster 1828: race; genus; species; generic class. The noun kind and the adjective kind (benevolent) are the same word by descent — to be kind is to act according to one’s kin — but in Genesis 1 the Authorized Version uses the noun, and it is a boundary word.
biblical_def: Kind is the creation account’s word for a fixed boundary, and it is repeated with such insistence that the repetition is itself the doctrine. Ten times in Genesis 1 the phrase falls: the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11); God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind (Genesis 1:21); Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind (Genesis 1:24). The Hebrew mīn marks a created category that reproduces within itself. Scripture does not tell us the taxonomic width of a kind, and the dictionary does not pretend it does; the text’s claim is narrower and firmer than a modern classification scheme. It says God made distinct categories, each bearing seed in itself, and that the categories are His and not an artifact of description. Paul assumes the same structure when arguing for the resurrection: All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds (1 Corinthians 15:39). The doctrine of creation and the doctrine of the resurrection body rest on the same premise — God assigns kinds, and He keeps them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KIND as a noun: race; genus; generic class; sort, in a sense more loose than genus. Webster derives it from the same root as kin, and notes the adjective sense — disposed to do good — grows from the idea of acting according to one’s nature or kindred.
webster_full: KIND, n. [Sax. cynd, kind, nature, kindred.] — Race; genus; generic class; as in Scripture, the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind. Sort, in a sense more loose than genus; as, a kind of stuff or silk. Nature; natural propensity or determination.

Webster cites Genesis directly under the noun, which tells us how the word was heard in 1828: kind was a category in nature, not a category in the mind of the classifier. That is the whole disagreement with the modern account, and it was already implicit in the dictionary two decades before the Origin of Species.
scriptures: Genesis 1:11
And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so.
Genesis 1:21
And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good.
Genesis 1:24
And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.
1 Corinthians 15:39
All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
corruption_summary: Kind is corrupted from a created boundary into a convenient human label — a name we assign to a slice of a continuum — which removes from Genesis 1 the one thing it repeats ten times, and which is then extended from biology to the body itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The Darwinian account does not merely propose a mechanism; it denies the category. If every living thing stands on an unbroken continuum, then kind is a word we impose on a gradient for convenience, and Genesis 1’s tenfold refrain describes nothing real. The dictionary’s position is that God created distinct kinds, each reproducing after itself, and that the boundaries are His. This is not a claim that the biblical kind maps onto the modern species — it plainly does not, and honest advocates on every side grant the mismatch. It is a claim that the categories are given rather than constructed. Everything in Genesis 1 that is repeated is repeated on purpose, and this phrase is repeated more than any other.

The deeper corruption arrives when the denial of created kinds is applied to man. Genesis 1:27 names two, male and female, in the same chapter and the same grammar that names the kinds of tree and beast. A generation taught that biological categories are labels laid over a continuum has been handed, in advance, the premise that the categories of sex are labels too — assignable, revisable, self-declared. The two claims are one claim. Scripture’s answer is the same in both cases and is stated as fact rather than opinion: male and female created he them. The boundary is creational, embodied, and not ours to move. Where a person suffers real distress against that boundary, the church owes compassion, patient care, and the gospel — and owes it precisely because the sufferer is an image-bearer of the God who fixed the kinds.
roots_summary: One Hebrew noun carries the weight in Genesis, and a Greek noun of family and stock carries it in the New Testament. Both name a lineage that breeds true, which is why the same vocabulary serves creation, clean-and-unclean law, and the resurrection argument.
roots_lines: Hebrew mīn (H4327) — kind, species, category; the boundary term of Genesis 1 and of the clean-and-unclean lists in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14.
Greek genos (G1085) — kind, race, family, stock, offspring; the root of English genus and generation.
The Hebrew phrase is l'mīnēhū, after his kind — a prepositional clause, not a bare noun, so the text speaks of reproduction according to a category rather than merely of a category.
Whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11) is the mechanism attached to the boundary: the kind is preserved because the seed is internal to it.
usage: Ten times in Genesis 1 creation proceeds after his kind — the most repeated phrase in the chapter, and therefore the most deliberate.
Whose seed is in itself (Genesis 1:11) ties the boundary to the means of its own preservation.
Paul argues the resurrection from the same premise: All flesh is not the same flesh (1 Corinthians 15:39). God assigns kinds, and He raises according to them.

etymology: Old English feohtan, to fight, to combat. Webster 1828: to strive or contend for victory in battle or single combat; to contend in arms. In the Authorized Version the word is used of literal war, of the LORD warring for His people, and — in Paul’s last letter — of the whole Christian life summed up in a single contest.
biblical_def: Scripture is not embarrassed by the verb fight, and it does not spiritualize it away. Israel fought real battles, and Nehemiah’s charge to men with trowels and swords is entirely concrete: Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses (Nehemiah 4:14). Yet the same Scripture insists the outcome is never the arm’s: The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace (Exodus 14:14). Those two verses are not in competition; they are the two halves of the doctrine. Men are commanded to stand and strike, and the victory belongs to God. Paul then takes the verb into the interior life without weakening it. He charges Timothy, Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life (1 Timothy 6:12), and near his own execution reports, I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). The Greek is agōnizomai, the athlete’s and soldier’s word for straining to the point of pain. And he insists the striving be aimed: so fight I, not as one that beateth the air (1 Corinthians 9:26). Sanctification is a contest, not a drift.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FIGHT as a verb: to strive or contend for victory in battle or in single combat; to attempt to defeat, subdue or destroy an enemy by blows or weapons. As a noun: a battle; an engagement; a contest in arms.
webster_full: FIGHT, v.i. [Sax. feohtan.] — To strive or contend for victory, in battle or in single combat; to attempt to defeat, subdue or destroy an enemy, either by blows or weapons. FIGHT, n. — A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms; a struggle for victory.

Webster allows no metaphorical softening: a fight is a struggle for victory against an enemy who must be subdued. When Paul says fight the good fight of faith, the Authorized Version’s readers heard exactly that, and the modern reader who hears only earnest effort has lost the noun enemy.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:12
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
2 Timothy 4:7
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
1 Corinthians 9:26
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air:
Exodus 14:14
The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace.
Nehemiah 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
corruption_summary: Fight is corrupted in two directions at once: quietism empties the command by leaning on Exodus 14:14 until the believer has nothing to do, while a rediscovered appetite for combat borrows the vocabulary of spiritual warfare for ordinary partisan aggression.
corruption_paragraphs: The quietist error takes The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace and generalizes a single moment at the Red Sea into the shape of the whole Christian life. Israel at the sea had no possible action; that is precisely why the word came. Six chapters later the same people are told to draw swords against Amalek, and Nehemiah arms every builder. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification holds both without strain: God works in the believer both to will and to do, and therefore the believer works out his own salvation with fear and trembling. A man who has stopped fighting sin because grace is sufficient has misread the same apostle who said I have fought a good fight when he had nothing left to gain by saying it.

The opposite corruption is louder now. Fight the good fight is quoted to sanctify contention that has no biblical object — factional combat inside congregations, or the ordinary aggressions of politics rebranded as spiritual warfare. Paul’s qualifier rules it out: so fight I, not as one that beateth the air. The good fight is defined by its object, which is faith, and by its weapons, which are not carnal. Nehemiah is instructive here rather than convenient: his men fought for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses — defence of the household and the people of God under lawful authority, not a search for enemies. A church that cannot tell the difference will find it has learned to swing without a target.
roots_summary: Two Greek words and one Hebrew word carry fight in the Authorized Version. The Hebrew is the plain verb for making war; the Greek pair comes from the contest ground and gives English agony and antagonist.
roots_lines: Greek agōnizomai (G75) — to contend for a prize, to struggle to the point of exhaustion (1 Timothy 6:12, fight the good fight).
Greek agōn (G73) — the contest, the struggle, the arena itself (2 Timothy 4:7, I have fought a good fight); the source of English agony.
Greek polemos (G4171) — war, battle; the word for armed conflict rather than contest, used of the wars of Revelation.
Hebrew lācham (H3898) — to fight, to do battle, to make war (Exodus 14:14, the LORD shall fight for you; Nehemiah 4:14).
usage: The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace (Exodus 14:14) — spoken where Israel could do nothing, not as a rule for every field.
Fight the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12): the contest is defined by its object, and its object is faith.
So fight I, not as one that beateth the air (1 Corinthians 9:26) — striving without aim is not zeal but noise.

etymology: Old English lōcian, to see, to behold, to gaze. Webster 1828: to direct the eye toward an object, with the intention of seeing it. In the Authorized Version look is frequently the whole of what a sinner is commanded to do — a verb chosen precisely because it contributes nothing to the object it rests on.
biblical_def: Look is the Bible’s cheapest verb and its most demanding. It is cheap because looking adds nothing to what is looked at; it is demanding because it requires a man to stop working on himself and turn his eyes outward. The pattern is set in the wilderness: Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived (Numbers 21:9). The dying were not asked to improve, to fight the venom, or to prove sincerity. They were asked to look. Isaiah universalizes it into the plainest gospel invitation in the Old Testament: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else (Isaiah 45:22). The Psalter records the effect on the face: They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed (Psalm 34:5). Micah makes it the posture of waiting under judgment: Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation (Micah 7:7). And Hebrews gives the Christian his fixed object for the whole race: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). The Greek there means looking away from everything else in order to look at one thing. Faith is not a stare into the self.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LOOK as a verb: to direct the eye toward an object, with the intention of seeing it; to direct the intellectual eye; to consider, to examine; to expect; and, with to or unto, to watch, to take care, to rely upon.
webster_full: LOOK, v.i. [Sax. locian.] — To direct the eye toward an object, with the intention of seeing it. To direct the intellectual eye; to consider; to examine. To expect. To take care; to watch. To be directed toward, as, the house looks to the north.

Webster’s last sense — direction, orientation, what a thing faces — is the biblical one. To look unto the LORD is not to glance at Him but to be turned toward Him, the way a house faces north whether or not anyone is at the window. That is why the verb can carry the weight of conversion without becoming a work.
scriptures: Isaiah 45:22
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.
Hebrews 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Numbers 21:9
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
Psalm 34:5
They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed.
Micah 7:7
Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.
corruption_summary: Look is corrupted when the direction of the gaze is reversed — when a verb Scripture always points outward toward God is turned inward toward the self, so that assurance is sought by examining one’s own looking rather than by looking.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic modern counsel is to look within: consult the heart, trust the inner voice, find the answer inside. Scripture’s verdict on that interior is that it is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, which makes it a poor place to search for salvation. Every scriptural use of this verb points the eye away from the man and onto God, a serpent of brass, or the Lord Jesus at the right hand of the throne. Isaiah does not say look into yourselves and be ye saved. The invitation is Look unto me, and the reason given is exclusive: for I am God, and there is none else. Any counsel that sends a troubled soul inward has reversed the only direction the Bible ever gives.

There is a subtler reversal that afflicts serious believers rather than careless ones: a man who has looked to Christ begins examining the quality of his looking, and assurance drains away into self-inspection. The bitten Israelite who kept checking whether he had looked properly would have died staring at his own eyes. Hebrews 12:2 answers this exactly — the object is Jesus, and He is named the author and finisher of our faith, which places both ends of the believer’s faith in His hands rather than the believer’s. Self-examination has a real and commanded place; the Supper requires it. But it is a periodic duty, not the posture of the Christian life, and it is never the ground of assurance. The ground is outside the man, on a pole, on a cross, on a throne.
roots_summary: Several Hebrew and Greek verbs stand behind look, and the useful distinction is between merely seeing and deliberately turning the eye. The New Testament’s word in Hebrews 12:2 is the strongest of them: it means to look away from one thing in order to look at another.
roots_lines: Hebrew nābat (H5027) — to look intently, to regard, to gaze upon with attention (Psalm 34:5, They looked unto him, and were lightened).
Greek aphoraō (G872) — to look away from all else and fix the eyes on one object (Hebrews 12:2, Looking unto Jesus). The turning away is part of the word.
Greek blepō (G991) — to see, to look at, to take heed; the ordinary verb of sight and of warning.
Greek anablepō (G308) — to look up, to recover sight; the word used when the blind receive their eyes and when Christ lifts His eyes to heaven.
usage: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth (Isaiah 45:22) — the verb is chosen because it adds nothing to its object.
The bitten Israelite beheld the serpent of brass and lived (Numbers 21:9); the cure was in the object, never in the quality of the gaze.
Looking unto Jesus (Hebrews 12:2) means looking away from everything else — including from oneself.

etymology: Past tense and participle of try, from Old French trier, to sift or pick out. Webster 1828 gives the older and stronger sense first: to examine by a test; to refine, as metal by fire; proved by experiment. The modern sense of try as attempt is late; in the Authorized Version tried almost always means assayed, and the assayer is God.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version tried is a metallurgist’s word, not an athlete’s. To be tried is to be put in the furnace so that what is genuine is separated from what is not, and Scripture assigns the furnace to God rather than to circumstance. Job, with every explanation taken from him, holds to this: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold (Job 23:10). He does not claim to understand the trial; he claims to know the assayer and the outcome. The Psalter applies the same image to Scripture itself: The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times (Psalm 12:6). Zechariah makes the refining covenantal, and notice what it produces: I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them (Zechariah 13:9). Peter gives the doctrine its New Testament form — the trial of faith is much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire (1 Peter 1:7). Gold survives the fire and then perishes anyway. Faith survives the fire and does not. That is the whole comparison.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TRIED as the past participle of try: proved by test or experiment; refined, as metal by fire; examined judicially; and as an adjective, having been proved reliable — a tried friend, a tried soldier.
webster_full: TRY, v.t. [Fr. trier, to pick out, to sift.] — To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test. To refine; to purify, as metals by melting. To examine judicially; to hear and determine. TRIED, pp. — Proved; refined; examined judicially.

Webster gives refine and examine judicially before he gives attempt, and both of the earlier senses are biblical. A man who is tried in Scripture has been assayed and has been judged, and in both cases something has been established about him that could not be established any other way.
scriptures: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
Psalm 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
1 Peter 1:7
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
Zechariah 13:9

And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It is my people: and they shall say, The LORD is my God.
Revelation 3:18

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
corruption_summary: Tried is corrupted when the biblical furnace — a purposeful refining governed by God — is replaced either by impersonal misfortune to be endured, or by a therapeutic account in which affliction exists chiefly to yield personal growth.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is practical rather than academic, and it is the one most believers actually fall into: suffering is treated as random damage, and the goal becomes recovery. Job’s confession refuses that framing while granting all of its pain. He knoweth the way that I take is not an explanation; Job never receives one. It is a claim about who is holding the crucible. The Reformed doctrine of providence says the same thing without the poetry: not a hair falls apart from the Father’s will, and He orders all things to His glory and His people’s good. The refining metaphor is exact on this point. Fire applied by no one is a house burning down. Fire applied by an assayer, at a governed temperature, for a set time, is a purification — and the difference lies entirely in whether there is someone at the furnace.

The second corruption keeps God in the picture but rewrites the purpose, so that the point of affliction becomes the sufferer’s own development — resilience, depth, a better version of the self. Peter states the end of the process differently: that the tried faith might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. The refining terminates on the day of Christ and on His praise, not on the believer’s improved condition in this life. Zechariah is blunter still: the fire produces a people who call on the name of the LORD and a God who answers It is my people. Growth is real and is genuinely given, but it is the byproduct. When it becomes the purpose, affliction is being measured by what it yields to the sufferer rather than by what it renders to God, and the comfort available to a Job — who got no growth narrative, only God — disappears.
roots_summary: The Hebrew has two distinct verbs behind tried, one for testing to discover and one for smelting to purify. The Greek adds a third idea, approval after examination. Together they describe a process with a purpose and a verdict, never a mishap.
roots_lines: Hebrew bāchan (H974) — to test, to examine, to prove, especially of metals and of hearts (Job 23:10; Psalm 12:6 context).
Hebrew tsāraph (H6884) — to smelt, to refine, to remove dross; the goldsmith’s and silversmith’s word (Zechariah 13:9, refine them as silver is refined).
Greek dokimazō (G1381) — to test with a view to approving; the assay that ends in a verdict of genuine (1 Peter 1:7).
Hebrew keseph (H3701) — silver; the metal of Psalm 12:6 and Zechariah 13:9, refined seven times, which is the number of completeness rather than a count.
usage: When he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold (Job 23:10) — Job names the assayer without receiving the explanation.
Scripture itself is as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times (Psalm 12:6): the word has already been through the fire the reader is entering.
Gold perisheth though it be tried with fire (1 Peter 1:7); tried faith does not. The comparison is about what survives the furnace and then survives.
